title: Interesting Interruptions
author: John Mark Reynolds
summary: John Mark Reynolds writes a reflective essay on fatherhood using Plato's Republic as an unexpected mirror, arguing that the interruptions of children are not distractions from a father's real work but often are the real work misidentified as an obstacle. He draws the key distinction from his own regret: years spent fixing home electronics so the family could stream movies felt urgent at the time, but in hindsight none of the moments he gave to his children were wasted and none of the work that displaced them mattered as much as he believed. The essay's organizing device is a close reading of three interruptions in Plato's Republic, at the start of Books II, IV, and V, where Socrates' students break into or resist the argument, and Reynolds credits Socrates' willingness to follow those interruptions rather than silence them as the source of the dialogue's greatest passages, including the philosopher-king, the divided line, and the cave allegory. From this he generalizes a rule for parenting, teaching, and any vocation: the difference between a harmful distraction and a meaningful interruption is whether the interruption serves the true end of the work, and a father, like Socrates, should treat a child's sincere approach as the lesson rather than a disruption of it. The piece closes on an explicitly devotional note, welcoming future interruptions from grown children and from God as more valuable than the uninterrupted completion of any task.
points: Reynolds's central claim is that a father's work is often mistaken for the interruption and the child's approach mistaken for the distraction, when in fact the relationship is the main thing and the auxiliary task is the true interruption.

He uses Plato's Republic as a structural parallel: three moments (Books II, IV, and V) where students interrupt Socrates, and argues Socrates' teaching greatness rests on treating those interruptions as the discussion's purpose rather than obstacles to it.

The essay credits the interruptions in Books II-V with producing some of Plato's most important ideas (the philosopher-king, the divided line, the cave allegory), framing pedagogical detours as generative rather than costly.

Reynolds distinguishes two kinds of interruption: the 'bad distraction' that pulls someone away from their true purpose (his Nehemiah example), and the misnamed 'interruption' that is actually the beginning of someone's real work or life (his Hobbit/Bilbo example).

The practical takeaway offered for parents, teachers, and leaders alike is that 'the lesson plan proposes, the student disposes' — a working principle for staying responsive to the person in front of you rather than the agenda.
quotes: The interruptions of our children were not interruptions, but life. "Beware," I think, "even now confusing the meaningful moments of life for interruptions.
The System must be built for the family, not the family for The System. In the world of home electronics and computers, I did not always remember this truth.
In education, learning is never a disruption. The student, if acting as a true student, is the class, not a disruption to the class.
He knows that the discussion is for the students, not the students for the discussion. In Book II the students interrupt and save the discussion from ending.
The distraction produces brilliance when the teacher followed the students and risked their misunderstandings, confusions, and questions.
When the dwarves turn up at Bilbo's front door in The Hobbit, this was not an interruption in Bilbo's life, but the beginning of his real life.
So it goes in parenting, education, business. The main thing, almost always a human or Divine thing, must remain the main thing.
